Pathology-01.question: ১) Most commonly involved site in phlebothrombosis is
Pathology-01.exp:
Phlebothrombosis refers to venous thrombosis, usually occurring in the deep veins of the lower limbs. The most common site is the deep veins of the lower extremity, especially the calf veins (e.g., posterior tibial and peroneal veins).

Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) is clinically important because thrombi may embolize to the lungs, causing pulmonary embolism.

Option Analysis

  • ক) Portal vein Portal vein thrombosis occurs in specific conditions (e.g., cirrhosis, malignancy) but is not the common site of phlebothrombosis.

  • খ) Lower extremity  Most common site of venous thrombosis.

  • গ) Upper extremity  Less common; may occur with central venous catheters or malignancy.

  • ঘ) Ovarian vein  Rare; may occur postpartum or with pelvic infection.

High-Yield Venous Thrombosis

Feature Fact
Most common site Deep veins of lower limb
Major complication Pulmonary embolism
Risk factors Virchow triad: stasis, endothelial injury, hypercoagulability

Rapid Recall

  • Phlebothrombosis → Lower limb DVT

  • DVT complication → Pulmonary embolism

  • Virchow triad → Stasis + Vessel injury + Hypercoagulability

Pathology-01.question: ২) Fat embolism is common in
Pathology-01.exp:
Fat embolism is most commonly associated with fractures of long bones, especially femur and tibia, and pelvic fractures. Fat droplets from damaged bone marrow enter the circulation and may cause fat embolism syndrome (FES).

Classic triad of Fat Embolism Syndrome:

  • Respiratory distress

  • Neurological symptoms (confusion, seizures)

  • Petechial rash

Option Analysis

  • ক) Fracture  Especially long-bone fractures.

  • খ) DVT  Causes thromboembolism (pulmonary embolism), not fat embolism.

  • গ) Blood transfusion Can cause transfusion reactions or air embolism (rare), not typical fat embolism.

  • ঘ) Thrombophlebitis Associated with thrombus formation and pulmonary embolism.

High-Yield Fat Embolism

Feature Finding
Common cause Long bone fracture
Onset Usually 24–72 hours after injury
Triad Respiratory distress + neurological signs + petechiae
Imaging "Snowstorm" appearance on chest X-ray

Rapid Recall

  • Fat embolism → Fracture of femur

  • Thromboembolism → DVT

  • Air embolism → Surgery/trauma/intravascular procedures

Pathology-01.question: ৩) White infarct occurs in
Pathology-01.exp:
A white (anaemic) infarct occurs when there is arterial occlusion in solid organs with end-arterial circulation, resulting in limited collateral blood supply. The classic sites are:

  • Spleen

  • Kidney

  • Heart

The infarct appears pale because there is little or no blood supply to the affected area.

Option Analysis

  • ক) Intestine  Usually develops a red (haemorrhagic) infarct because of dual blood supply and loose tissue structure.

  • খ) Spleen Classic site of white infarction.

  • গ) Lung  Usually develops red infarction due to dual blood supply (pulmonary and bronchial circulation).

  • ঘ) Ovary  Torsion may cause haemorrhagic infarction rather than classic white infarction.

Rapid Recall

  • White infarct → Heart + Kidney + Spleen

  • Red infarct → Lung + Intestine

  • Solid organ with end-artery → White infarct

Pathology-01.question: ৪) Malignant tumour arising from mesenchymal tissue is called
Pathology-01.exp:
A sarcoma is a malignant tumour arising from mesenchymal (connective tissue) origin. Mesenchymal tissues include bone, cartilage, muscle, fat, blood vessels, and fibrous tissue.

Examples:

  • Osteosarcoma → bone

  • Chondrosarcoma → cartilage

  • Leiomyosarcoma → smooth muscle

  • Liposarcoma → adipose tissue

Option Analysis

  • ক) Carcinoma  Malignant tumour arising from epithelial tissue (e.g., skin, glands, mucosa).

  • খ) Hematoma  A collection of blood due to bleeding, not a tumour.

  • গ) Sarcoma  Malignant tumour of mesenchymal origin.

  • ঘ) Adenoma  Benign tumour arising from glandular epithelium.

Rapid Recall

  • Carcinoma → Epithelial origin

  • Sarcoma → Mesenchymal origin

  • "Sarcoma = Soft tissue/bone malignancy"

Pathology-01.question: ৫) Feature of anaplastic tumour is
Pathology-01.exp:
Anaplastic tumours are malignant tumours showing poor differentiation and loss of normal cellular features. A hallmark feature is pleomorphism, meaning marked variation in cell size and shape.

Other features of anaplasia include:

  • Hyperchromatic nuclei

  • Increased nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio

  • Abnormal mitotic figures

  • Loss of polarity

  • Giant tumour cells

Option Analysis

  • ক) Normal nuclear morphology  Anaplastic cells show abnormal nuclear features.

  • খ) Pleomorphism  Classic feature of anaplasia.

  • গ) Typical mitotic figure  Malignant anaplastic tumours show atypical mitotic figures.

  • ঘ) Normal polarity  Loss of cellular polarity is a feature of anaplasia.

High-Yield Features of Anaplasia

Feature Finding
Differentiation Poor/absent
Nuclear morphology Abnormal
Cell shape Pleomorphism
Mitosis Increased + atypical
Polarity Lost

Rapid Recall

Anaplasia = 4 A’s

  • Atypical mitosis

  • Anisonucleosis/pleomorphism

  • Abnormal nuclei

  • Absent polarity

Pathology-01.question: ৬) Carcinoma in situ includes
Pathology-01.exp:
Carcinoma in situ (CIS) refers to severe epithelial dysplasia involving the full thickness of epithelium without invasion through the basement membrane.

Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is a classic example of carcinoma in situ, particularly CIN III (high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion).

Option Analysis

  • ক) CIN  A premalignant/in situ lesion of cervical epithelium.

  • খ) Pernicious anaemia  A condition causing vitamin B12 deficiency and increased risk of gastric carcinoma, but not carcinoma in situ.

  • গ) Chronic gastritis  A risk factor for gastric carcinoma through atrophy and intestinal metaplasia, not CIS.

  • ঘ) Cirrhosis of liver  A risk factor for hepatocellular carcinoma, not carcinoma in situ.

High-Yield Carcinoma in Situ

Site Example
Cervix CIN III
Skin Bowen disease
Breast Ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS)

Rapid Recall

  • CIS = Full-thickness dysplasia + intact basement membrane

  • CIN III → Cervical carcinoma in situ

  • Invasion beyond basement membrane = invasive carcinoma

Pathology-01.question: ৭) Carcinoma of breast metastasizes
Pathology-01.exp:
Breast carcinoma most commonly metastasizes through the lymphatic route, especially to the axillary lymph nodes. Lymphatic spread is an important pathway for staging and prognosis assessment in breast cancer.

Common lymphatic drainage:

  • Axillary lymph nodes (most common)

  • Internal mammary nodes

  • Supraclavicular nodes

Option Analysis

  • ক) Lymphatic route  Most common route of breast carcinoma spread.

  • খ) Hematogenous route  Occurs later, commonly spreading to bone, lung, liver, and brain.

  • গ) Direct seeding of surfaces Typical of tumours spreading across serosal surfaces (e.g., ovarian carcinoma).

  • ঘ) Indirect seeding of cavity Not a typical metastatic pathway for breast carcinoma.

High-Yield Routes of Tumour Metastasis

Route Example
Lymphatic Breast carcinoma → Axillary nodes
Haematogenous Sarcomas, breast cancer → bone/lung
Transcoelomic (seeding) Ovarian carcinoma → peritoneum

Rapid Recall

  • Breast cancer → Lymphatics → Axillary lymph nodes

  • Sarcoma → Blood vessels

  • Ovarian cancer → Peritoneal seeding

Pathology-01.question: ৮) Tumour suppressor gene responsible for cell cycle arrest is
Pathology-01.exp:
p53 is a major tumour suppressor gene responsible for cell cycle arrest in response to DNA damage. It is known as the "guardian of the genome".

Mechanism:

  • DNA damage → p53 activation

  • p53 increases p21 expression

  • p21 inhibits cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs)

  • Cell cycle is arrested (mainly at G1/S checkpoint)

  • Allows DNA repair or induces apoptosis if damage is severe

Option Analysis

  • ক) p53 Controls G1/S cell cycle arrest and apoptosis.

  • খ) BRCA1  Tumour suppressor involved in DNA repair, especially breast and ovarian cancer susceptibility.

  • গ) RB1  Controls the G1/S checkpoint by regulating the release of E2F transcription factors; also a tumour suppressor but less classically described as the DNA damage "guardian".

  • ঘ) WT1  Tumour suppressor associated with Wilms tumour.

Rapid Recall

  • p53 → Guardian of genome → Cell cycle arrest + apoptosis

  • RB1 → G1/S checkpoint brake

  • BRCA → DNA repair

  • WT1 → Wilms tumour

Pathology-01.question: ৯) HHV-8 is responsible for
Pathology-01.exp:
Human herpesvirus-8 (HHV-8), also known as Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV), is responsible for Kaposi sarcoma, particularly in immunocompromised patients such as those with HIV/AIDS.

Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumour characterised by:

  • Spindle cells

  • Vascular proliferation

  • Red-purple skin lesions

Option Analysis

  • ক) Burkitt lymphoma  Associated with Epstein–Barr virus (EBV) and MYC translocation t(8;14).

  • খ) Kaposi sarcoma  Caused by HHV-8.

  • গ) Carcinoma of cervix  Associated with high-risk HPV (especially HPV 16 and 18).

  • ঘ) Lymphoma  Some lymphomas are associated with EBV or HHV-8 (e.g., primary effusion lymphoma), but the classic association is Kaposi sarcoma.

Rapid Recall

  • HHV-8 → Kaposi sarcoma

  • EBV → Burkitt lymphoma

  • HPV → Cervical carcinoma

  • HTLV-1 → Adult T-cell lymphoma

Pathology-01.question: ১০) FIGO staging system is used for staging of
Pathology-01.exp:
The FIGO (International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics) staging system is used for staging gynaecological malignancies, including ovarian cancer, cervical cancer, and endometrial cancer.

For ovarian carcinoma, FIGO staging is based mainly on the extent of tumour spread:

  • Stage I → Confined to ovaries/fallopian tubes

  • Stage II → Pelvic extension

  • Stage III → Peritoneal spread outside pelvis and/or regional lymph nodes

  • Stage IV → Distant metastasis

Option Analysis

  • ক) Ca breast  Uses TNM staging system mainly.

  • খ) Ca lung  Uses TNM staging system.

  • গ) Ovarian Ca  FIGO staging is classically used.

  • ঘ) Lymphoma  Uses Ann Arbor staging system.

Rapid Recall

  • FIGO → Gynaecological cancers

  • TNM → Most solid tumours

  • Ann Arbor → Lymphoma

Pathology-01.question: ১১) Pre-cancerous condition includes
Pathology-01.exp:
Villous adenoma is a precancerous (premalignant) lesion of the colon with a significant risk of progression to colorectal carcinoma, especially when large or showing high-grade dysplasia.

The adenoma–carcinoma sequence:
Normal mucosa → Adenoma → Dysplasia → Colorectal carcinoma

Option Analysis

  • ক) Villous adenoma  A premalignant colorectal polyp with high malignant potential.

  • খ) Lymphoid polyp  Usually benign and not associated with malignant transformation.

  • গ) Metaplastic polyp  Generally benign with minimal or no malignant potential.

  • ঘ) Hamartomatous polyp Usually benign, although some syndromic hamartomatous polyps may carry increased cancer risk.

Rapid Recall

  • Villous adenoma → Premalignant → Colorectal carcinoma risk

  • Most common adenomatous polyp → Tubular adenoma

  • Highest malignant potential → Villous adenoma

Pathology-01.question: ১২) Time (in minute) for autoclaving
১৩) Leukocyte migration through endothelium is called-
Pathology-01.exp:
Diapedesis is the process by which leukocytes migrate through the endothelial lining of blood vessels and enter the surrounding tissue during inflammation.

The sequence of leukocyte recruitment is:

Margination → Rolling → Adhesion → Diapedesis → Chemotaxis → Phagocytosis

Option Analysis

  • ক) Phagocytosis  Engulfment and destruction of microbes or cellular debris by leukocytes.

  • খ) Chemotaxis  Movement of leukocytes towards chemical signals after leaving the vessel.

  • গ) Diapedesis  Passage of leukocytes through endothelium into tissues.

  • ঘ) Margination Movement of leukocytes from the central blood flow toward the vessel wall.

Rapid Recall

  • Diapedesis = WBC exit from blood vessel

  • Chemotaxis = WBC movement toward chemicals

  • Phagocytosis = WBC eating microbes

Pathology-01.question: ১৪) ROS are produced within
Pathology-01.exp:
Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are mainly produced in the mitochondria during normal cellular respiration, especially at the electron transport chain (ETC) where oxygen is reduced to form superoxide radicals.

Important ROS include:

  • Superoxide anion (O₂⁻)

  • Hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂)

  • Hydroxyl radical (OH⁻)

Excess ROS causes oxidative stress and contributes to cell injury.

Option Analysis

  • ক) Mitochondria  Major intracellular source of ROS during oxidative phosphorylation.

  • খ) Lysosome  Contains hydrolytic enzymes for intracellular digestion; not the main ROS source.

  • গ) Ribosome  Responsible for protein synthesis.

  • ঘ) Endoplasmic reticulum  Can generate some ROS during protein folding, but mitochondria are the major source.

Rapid Recall

  • ROS → Mitochondria

  • ATP → Mitochondria

  • Protein synthesis → Ribosome

  • Intracellular digestion → Lysosome

Pathology-01.question: ১৫) The richest source of histamine is
Pathology-01.exp:
Mast cells are the richest source of histamine in the body. They are abundant in connective tissues, especially around blood vessels and nerves, and play a major role in Type-I hypersensitivity reactions.

On activation (e.g., by allergen-mediated IgE cross-linking), mast cells release:

  • Histamine

  • Leukotrienes

  • Prostaglandins

  • Cytokines

Option Analysis

  • ক) Mast cell  Main storage site and richest source of histamine.

  • খ) Platelet  Can release some histamine but is not the major source.

  • গ) Basophil  Contains histamine and participates in allergic reactions, but less abundant than mast cells.

  • ঘ) RBC  Does not store histamine.

Rapid Recall

  • Histamine richest source → Mast cell

  • Immediate allergy/anaphylaxis → Mast cell degranulation

  • Type-I hypersensitivity → IgE + Mast cell

Pathology-01.question: ১৬) Permanent tissue includes
Pathology-01.exp:
Permanent tissues (permanent cells) are cells that lose the ability to divide after maturation and remain in the G₀ phase of the cell cycle. Skeletal muscle cells are considered permanent cells because they have very limited regenerative capacity.

Option Analysis

  • ক) Epithelium of GIT  A labile tissue with continuous cell division and rapid regeneration.

  • খ) Mesenchymal cells  Generally considered stable cells with regenerative capacity.

  • গ) Vascular endothelial cells  Stable cells that can proliferate during repair and angiogenesis.

  • ঘ) Skeletal muscle  A permanent tissue with minimal regenerative capacity.

Rapid Recall

  • Permanent cells → Neurons + Cardiac muscle + Skeletal muscle

  • Labile cells → GIT epithelium + Bone marrow

  • Stable cells → Liver + Endothelium

Pathology-01.question: ১৭) Surgical gowns are sterilized by
১৮) Which one is the hallmark of malignancy?
Pathology-01.exp:
The hallmark of malignancy is the ability of a tumour to metastasize, i.e., spread to distant sites through lymphatic or blood vessels. Metastasis distinguishes a malignant tumour from a benign tumour.

Option Analysis

  • ক) Rapid growth  Not specific for malignancy; some benign tumours can grow rapidly.

  • খ) Anaplasia  A feature of malignant tumours showing poor differentiation, but not the defining hallmark.

  • গ) Metastasis Most reliable evidence of malignancy.

  • ঘ) Local invasion  Malignant tumours commonly invade locally, but metastasis is the hallmark feature.

Rapid Recall

  • Benign vs malignant → Metastasis is the key differentiator

  • Anaplasia = poor differentiation

  • Metastasis = definite evidence of malignancy

Pathology-01.question: ১৯) Criteria of benign tumour
২০) Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma is associated with
২১) Most common site of fatty change is
Pathology-01.exp:
The liver is the most common site of fatty change (fatty degeneration/steatosis) because hepatocytes are actively involved in fat metabolism, including fatty acid uptake, synthesis, oxidation, and lipoprotein production.

Fatty change occurs when there is an imbalance between:

  • Fatty acid entry and synthesis

  • Fatty acid oxidation

  • Lipoprotein export

Common causes:

  • Alcohol abuse

  • Obesity

  • Diabetes mellitus

  • Hypoxia

  • Toxins

Option Analysis

  • ক) Liver  common and most commonly affected organ by fatty change.

  • খ) Kidney  Can develop fatty change but is not the commonest site.

  • গ) Spleen  Not a typical site of fatty change.

  • ঘ) Heart  May show fatty degeneration (e.g., "tiger heart" in hypoxia), but less common than liver.

Rapid Recall

  • Fatty change → Liver

  • Most common cause of fatty liver → Alcohol/metabolic syndrome

  • "Tiger heart" → Fatty degeneration of myocardium

Pathology-01.question: ২২) Cellular aging results from
Pathology-01.exp:
Cellular aging (senescence) occurs mainly due to progressive shortening of telomeres with repeated cell division. When telomeres become critically short, cells enter a state of replicative senescence and lose the ability to divide.

Telomeres are protective DNA sequences at the ends of chromosomes maintained by telomerase. Most somatic cells have limited telomerase activity, leading to gradual telomere shortening.

Option Analysis

  • ক) RNA repair defect  Not the major mechanism of cellular aging.

  • খ) Telomere shortening  Major cause of replicative cellular senescence.

  • গ) Normal growth factor signalling  Maintains normal cellular function, not aging.

  • ঘ) Telomere lengthening  Promotes continued cell division and is associated with immortalization of cancer cells.

Rapid Recall

  • Cell aging → Telomere shortening

  • Cancer cells → Telomerase activation → Telomere maintenance

  • Senescence = irreversible cell cycle arrest

Pathology-01.question: ২৩) Predominant acute inflammatory cell in first 24 hours is
Pathology-01.exp:
The predominant inflammatory cell in the first 24 hours of acute inflammation is the neutrophil (polymorphonuclear leukocyte, PMN).

Neutrophils are the first responders because they:

  • Rapidly migrate to the site of injury

  • Perform phagocytosis

  • Release antimicrobial substances and enzymes

After about 24–48 hours, monocytes/macrophages become predominant.

Option Analysis

  • ক) Monocyte  Predominates later (after 24–48 hours) and transforms into macrophages.

  • খ) Lymphocyte  Seen mainly in chronic inflammation and some viral infections.

  • গ) Neutrophil  First predominant cell in acute inflammation.

  • ঘ) Eosinophil  Associated with allergic reactions and parasitic infections.

Rapid Recall

  • Acute inflammation → Neutrophil

  • Chronic inflammation → Lymphocyte + macrophage

  • Allergy → Eosinophil

Pathology-01.question: ২৪) Beneficial effect of inflammation is
Pathology-01.exp:
The main beneficial effect of inflammation is to eliminate the cause of injury, especially infectious agents, and initiate the process of tissue repair.

Inflammation helps by:

  • Recruiting leukocytes (especially neutrophils in acute inflammation)

  • Destroying microbes through phagocytosis

  • Removing damaged tissue

  • Initiating healing and repair

Option Analysis

  • ক) Disfiguring scar A possible harmful consequence of excessive or prolonged inflammation.

  • খ) Endothelial cell injury  A harmful effect that may occur during inflammation.

  • গ) Control of infection Major protective role of inflammation.

  • ঘ) Tissue damage  A harmful consequence of uncontrolled inflammation.

    Rapid Recall

    • Inflammation = Defence + Repair

    • Benefit → Control infection

    • Excess inflammation → Tissue damage

Pathology-01.question: ২৫) Criteria of acute inflammation
২৬) Molecules involved in ARDS
Pathology-01.exp:
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is caused by an intense inflammatory response in the lungs. The key molecules involved are pro-inflammatory cytokines, which activate neutrophils and increase pulmonary endothelial and alveolar epithelial injury.

Important cytokines:

  • TNF-α

  • IL-1

  • IL-6

  • IL-8 (neutrophil recruitment)

This leads to:

  • Diffuse alveolar damage

  • Increased vascular permeability

  • Pulmonary oedema

  • Severe hypoxaemia

Pathology-01.question: ২৭) Which metabolite of arachidonic acid increases vascular permeability?
Pathology-01.exp:
Leukotrienes C4 (LTC4) are metabolites of arachidonic acid that increase vascular permeability by causing endothelial contraction and widening of intercellular gaps.

The cysteinyl leukotrienes:

  • LTC4

  • LTD4

  • LTE4

cause:

  • ↑ Vascular permeability

  • Bronchoconstriction

  • Smooth muscle contraction

Rapid Recall

  • LTC4 → Leak (vascular permeability)

  • LTB4 → Leukocyte migration

  • TXA2 → Thrombosis

  • PGI2 → Protection from platelet aggregation

Pathology-01.question: ২৮) Shrinkage in size of cell by loss of cell substance is called
Pathology-01.exp:
Atrophy is the shrinkage of a cell or organ due to loss of cell substance. It occurs when cells decrease in size due to reduced structural components, such as proteins and organelles.

Causes of atrophy:

  • Disuse (e.g., immobilized limb)

  • Loss of nerve supply (denervation)

  • Reduced blood supply (ischaemia)

  • Malnutrition

  • Loss of endocrine stimulation

Option Analysis

  • ক) Atrophy  Reduction in cell size due to loss of cellular components.

  • খ) Hypertrophy  Increase in cell size due to increased workload or hormonal stimulation.

  • গ) Metaplasia  Reversible change from one mature cell type to another.

  • ঘ) Anaplasia  Loss of differentiation, a feature of malignant tumours.

Rapid Recall

Pathology-01.question: ২৯) Pathological hypertrophy occurs in
Pathology-01.option4: Hypertrophy of skeletal muscle in body builder
Pathology-01.exp:
Pathological hypertrophy is an increase in cell size due to abnormal stress or disease conditions. Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) occurs due to chronic pressure overload, commonly from hypertension or aortic stenosis.

Option Analysis

  • ক) Left ventricular hypertrophy ✔ Correct. A classic example of pathological hypertrophy due to increased cardiac workload.

  • খ) Hypertrophy of pregnant uterus Physiological hypertrophy due to hormonal stimulation (oestrogen).

  • গ) Hypertrophy of breast during lactation  Physiological adaptation due to hormonal stimulation.

  • ঘ) Hypertrophy of skeletal muscle in body builder  Physiological hypertrophy due to increased workload/exercise.

High-Yield Hypertrophy

Type Example
Pathological hypertrophy LVH in hypertension, aortic stenosis
Physiological hypertrophy Pregnancy uterus, skeletal muscle in athletes

Rapid Recall

  • Heart under pressure → Pathological hypertrophy

  • Exercise/pregnancy → Physiological hypertrophy

  • Hypertrophy = ↑ cell size (not cell number)

Pathology-01.question: ৩০) Connective tissue metaplasia occurs in
Pathology-01.exp:
Connective tissue metaplasia is the transformation of one type of connective tissue into another, usually involving formation of bone or cartilage in soft tissues.

Myositis ossificans is a classic example where fibroblasts in muscle tissue differentiate into osteoblasts, leading to heterotopic bone formation.

Option Analysis

  • ক) Myositis ossificans  Example of connective tissue metaplasia (bone formation in soft tissue).

  • খ) Bile duct obstruction  Causes cholestasis and liver injury, not connective tissue metaplasia.

  • গ) Habitual smoker  Causes squamous metaplasia of respiratory epithelium.

  • ঘ) Barrett oesophagus  Causes columnar metaplasia of oesophageal squamous epithelium.

High-Yield Metaplasia Examples

Type Example
Connective tissue metaplasia Myositis ossificans
Squamous metaplasia Smoker’s bronchus
Columnar metaplasia Barrett oesophagus

Rapid Recall

  • Myositis ossificans → Bone formation in muscle → Connective tissue metaplasia

  • Smoking → Squamous metaplasia

  • Barrett oesophagus → Columnar metaplasia

Pathology-01.question: ৩১) Normal cellular constituent that accumulates inside the cell is
Pathology-01.exp:
Lipid is a normal cellular constituent that can accumulate inside cells as a form of intracellular accumulation (fatty change/steatosis) when cellular metabolism is disturbed.

Examples:

  • Triglyceride accumulation in hepatocytes → fatty liver

  • Lipid accumulation in other cells due to metabolic abnormalities

Option Analysis

  • ক) Product of infectious agent  An example of an exogenous/pathological substance, not a normal cellular constituent.

  • খ) Hemosiderin  An intracellular accumulation of haemoglobin-derived pigment, considered an abnormal pigment accumulation.

  • গ) Melanin  A normal pigment produced by melanocytes, but not a typical accumulated cellular constituent causing degeneration.

  • ঘ) Lipid . A normal cellular component that may accumulate intracellularly.

High-Yield Intracellular Accumulations

Type Example
Normal cellular constituent Lipid, glycogen
Endogenous abnormal pigment Hemosiderin, bilirubin
Exogenous pigment Carbon pigment

Rapid Recall

  • Fatty change = intracellular lipid accumulation

  • Hemosiderin = iron storage pigment

  • Melanin = normal pigment

Pathology-01.question: ৩২) Gumma is found in
৩৩) Healing by secondary intention occurs in-
Pathology-01.exp:
Healing by secondary intention occurs when there is a large tissue defect with wound edges not approximated, such as complicated, infected, or contaminated wounds.

Features of secondary intention:

  • More extensive inflammation

  • Greater granulation tissue formation

  • More wound contraction

  • Larger scar formation

Option Analysis

  • ক) Complicated wound Heals by secondary intention due to large tissue loss or poor wound approximation.

  • খ) Simple wound  Usually heals by primary intention.

  • গ) Small incised wound  Heals by primary intention.

  • ঘ) Clean incised wound  Classic example of primary intention healing.

Rapid Recall

  • Clean surgical wound → Primary intention

  • Large contaminated wound → Secondary intention

  • Secondary intention = More scar + more contraction

Pathology-01.question: ৩৪) Granulation tissue is composed of
Pathology-01.exp:
Granulation tissue is a newly formed vascular connective tissue that appears during wound healing. It is mainly composed of:

  • Fibroblasts → produce collagen and extracellular matrix

  • New capillaries (angiogenesis) → give the tissue a granular appearance

  • Inflammatory cells (mainly macrophages)

Option Analysis

  • ক) Epithelioid cell  Seen in granulomatous inflammation (e.g., tuberculosis).

  • খ) Langhans type giant cell  A feature of granulomas, especially TB.

  • গ) Fibroblast  Major cell responsible for collagen deposition in granulation tissue.

  • ঘ) Basophil  Involved in allergic reactions, not granulation tissue formation.

High-Yield Granulation Tissue

Components:

  1. Fibroblasts → collagen synthesis

  2. Endothelial cells → new blood vessel formation

  3. Macrophages → growth factors and debris removal

Rapid Recall

  • Granulation tissue ≠ granuloma

  • Granulation tissue → Fibroblast + capillaries + macrophages

  • Granuloma → Epithelioid cells + giant cells

Pathology-01.question: ৩৫) Complication of wound healing due to deficient scar formation is
Pathology-01.exp:
Wound dehiscence is a complication of wound healing due to deficient scar formation, resulting in separation or rupture of wound edges after closure.

Common causes:

  • Poor collagen synthesis

  • Infection

  • Excessive mechanical stress

  • Malnutrition (especially vitamin C deficiency)

  • Steroid therapy

Option Analysis

  • ক) Desmoids  Due to excessive proliferation of fibroblasts causing abnormal scar-like tumour formation.

  • খ) Proud flesh  Represents excessive granulation tissue formation (overgrowth of granulation tissue).

  • গ) Hypertrophic scar  Due to excessive collagen deposition during healing.

  • ঘ) Wound dehiscence  Occurs due to inadequate scar strength.

High-Yield Complications of Wound Healing

Problem Mechanism
Wound dehiscence Deficient scar formation
Hypertrophic scar Excess collagen deposition
Keloid Excess collagen extending beyond wound margin
Proud flesh Excess granulation tissue

Rapid Recall

  • Too little scar → Wound dehiscence

  • Too much scar → Hypertrophic scar/keloid

  • Excess granulation tissue → Proud flesh

Pathology-01.question: ৩৬) Most common cause of thrombosis is
Pathology-01.exp:
The most common and important initiating factor in thrombosis is endothelial injury. It exposes subendothelial collagen and tissue factor, leading to platelet adhesion, activation of coagulation pathways, and thrombus formation.

Virchow’s triad of thrombosis:

  1. Endothelial injury (most important in arterial thrombosis)

  2. Abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence)

  3. Hypercoagulability

Option Analysis

  • ক) Endothelial injury Major initiating mechanism for thrombus formation.

  • খ) Stasis Important in venous thrombosis (e.g., DVT), but not the overall most common initiating factor.

  • গ) Hypercoagulability of blood  A contributing factor, especially in inherited/acquired thrombophilia.

  • ঘ) Turbulent blood flow  Contributes to thrombosis but less important than endothelial injury.

High-Yield Virchow’s Triad

Factor Example
Endothelial injury Atherosclerosis, vessel trauma
Abnormal flow Aneurysm, atrial fibrillation, DVT
Hypercoagulability Factor V Leiden, malignancy

Rapid Recall

  • Thrombosis = Virchow triad

  • Most important initiating factor → Endothelial injury

  • DVT → Stasis

  • Arterial thrombus → Endothelial injury

Pathology-01.question: ৩৭) Which one is double edged sword?
Pathology-01.exp:
Metaplasia is considered a "double-edged sword" because it is a protective adaptive response but may also increase the risk of malignant transformation if the stimulus persists.

Example:

  • Barrett oesophagus: chronic acid reflux causes squamous epithelium to change into columnar epithelium → protective adaptation, but increases risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

  • Smoking-induced bronchial squamous metaplasia → protective initially, but may progress to dysplasia and carcinoma.

Option Analysis

  • ক) Atrophy  Reduction in cell size due to loss of cell substance; usually an adaptive response.

  • খ) Hypertrophy  Increase in cell size due to increased workload; may become harmful if excessive (e.g., LVH), but not classically called a double-edged sword.

  • গ) Hyperplasia  Increase in cell number; may be physiological or pathological, but not the classic answer.

  • ঘ) Metaplasia Protective adaptation with potential malignant risk.

High-Yield Cellular Adaptations

Adaptation Example Risk
Atrophy Disuse muscle wasting Loss of function
Hypertrophy LVH in hypertension Heart failure
Hyperplasia Endometrial hyperplasia Possible malignancy
Metaplasia Barrett oesophagus Dysplasia/cancer

Rapid Recall

Metaplasia = Adaptation + Cancer risk → Double-edged sword

Pathology-01.question: ৩৮) Activation of complement can be induced by -
Pathology-01.exp:
Complement activation through the classical pathway is induced mainly by antigen–antibody complexes, especially antibodies of the IgM and IgG classes.

Among the options, IgM is the most powerful activator of complement because a single IgM molecule can efficiently bind and activate the C1 component of complement.

Option Analysis

  • ক) IgD  Mainly functions as a B-cell receptor; does not significantly activate complement.

  • খ) IgM  Strongest activator of the classical complement pathway.

  • গ) IgA  Important in mucosal immunity; mainly activates alternative/lectin pathways weakly in some contexts.

  • ঘ) IgE  Involved in Type-I hypersensitivity and mast cell activation.

High-Yield Immunoglobulin Functions

Immunoglobulin Key Function
IgM Strongest complement activation
IgG Opsonization + complement activation
IgA Mucosal immunity
IgE Allergy + parasites
IgD B-cell activation

Rapid Recall

  • IgM → Maximum complement activation

  • IgG → Opsonization

  • IgA → Secretions

  • IgE → Allergy

Pathology-01.question: ৩৯) Central tolerance of the immune system takes place in -
Pathology-01.exp:
Reference: Lange mic

Central tolerance is the process by which developing immature lymphocytes that recognize self-antigens are eliminated or inactivated to prevent autoimmunity.

Sites of central tolerance:

  • B cells → Bone marrow

  • T cells → Thymus

Among the given options, bone marrow is the correct answer.

Option Analysis

  • ক) Bone marrow  Site of B-cell development and central tolerance.

  • খ) Lymph nodes  Site of peripheral tolerance and immune activation.

  • গ) Spleen  Secondary lymphoid organ; involved in peripheral immune responses.

  • ঘ) Tonsils  Secondary lymphoid tissue involved in mucosal immunity.

Rapid Recall

  • T-cell central tolerance → Thymus

  • B-cell central tolerance → Bone marrow

  • Peripheral tolerance → Lymph node + spleen

robiology/14th/P-568

Pathology-01.question: ৪০) Memory cells are present in case of -
Pathology-01.exp:
Memory cells are long-lived immune cells formed after the first exposure to an antigen. They provide a faster and stronger response during subsequent exposure (secondary immune response).

B lymphocytes differentiate into:

  • Plasma cells → produce antibodies

  • Memory B cells → provide long-term immunity

Option Analysis

  • ক) Eosinophil  Involved mainly in parasitic infections and allergic reactions; no memory function.

  • খ) B lymphocyte  Forms memory B cells responsible for immunological memory.

  • গ) Mast cell  Involved in immediate hypersensitivity; does not form classical memory cells.

  • ঘ) Macrophage  Phagocytic cells involved in innate immunity.

High-Yield Immunological Memory

Cell Function
Memory B cell Long-term antibody-mediated immunity
Memory T cell Long-term cell-mediated immunity
Plasma cell Antibody secretion

Rapid Recall

  • Memory cells → B lymphocytes + T lymphocytes

  • Antibody production → B cell → Plasma cell

  • Secondary immune response → Memory cells

Pathology-01.question: ৪১) Steps of extravasation in lumen excluding-?
Pathology-01.exp:
Extravasation refers to the process by which leukocytes move from the bloodstream into tissues during inflammation. The steps occurring within the vessel lumen are:

  1. Margination → leukocytes move toward vessel wall

  2. Rolling → selectin-mediated weak attachment

  3. Adhesion → integrin-mediated firm attachment

After crossing the endothelium (diapedesis), leukocytes undergo chemotaxis toward the site of injury.

Option Analysis

  • ক) Margination  A step of leukocyte extravasation in the vessel lumen.

  • খ) Rolling  A step occurring in the vessel lumen.

  • গ) Adhesion  A step occurring on the endothelial surface.

  • ঘ) Chemotaxis  Occurs after extravasation in the tissue, not in the lumen.

High-Yield Leukocyte Recruitment Sequence

Margination → Rolling → Adhesion → Diapedesis → Chemotaxis → Phagocytosis

Rapid Recall

  • Lumen steps → Margination + Rolling + Adhesion

  • Through vessel wall → Diapedesis

  • In tissue → Chemotaxis

Pathology-01.question: ৪২) Most common form of graft rejection
Pathology-01.exp:
The most common form of graft rejection is acute cellular rejection, which is mediated mainly by T lymphocytes attacking the transplanted tissue.

It typically occurs:

  • Days to months after transplantation

  • Due to activation of recipient T cells

  • Causes graft inflammation and tissue injury

Option Analysis

  • ক) Acute humoral rejection  Mediated by antibodies; less common than acute cellular rejection.

  • খ) Hyperacute rejection  Occurs within minutes to hours due to preformed antibodies against donor antigens.

  • গ) Acute cellular rejection  Most common type of graft rejection.

  • ঘ) Chronic allograft failure  Occurs months to years later due to chronic immune-mediated vascular injury and fibrosis.

Rapid Recall

  • Most common graft rejection → Acute cellular rejection

  • Hyperacute → Preformed antibody

  • Acute cellular → T cells

  • Chronic → Fibrosis and graft failure

Pathology-01.question: ৪৩) In which disease failure of thymic development occur ?
Pathology-01.exp:
Reference: Davidson 23rd

DiGeorge syndrome (22q11 deletion syndrome) occurs due to failure of development of the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches, leading to thymic aplasia or hypoplasia.

Consequences:

  • ↓ T lymphocytes

  • Impaired cell-mediated immunity

  • Increased susceptibility to viral and fungal infections

Classic features:

  • CATCH-22

    • Cardiac defects

    • Abnormal facies

    • Thymic aplasia

    • Cleft palate

    • Hypocalcaemia

Option Analysis

  • ক) Common variable immune deficiency  Mainly causes impaired antibody production with low immunoglobulins.

  • খ) Severe combined immune deficiency (SCID)  Causes severe defects in both T and B cell immunity, but not specifically due to thymic development failure.

  • গ) Selective IgA deficiency Causes isolated IgA deficiency.

  • ঘ) DiGeorge syndrome Due to thymic developmental failure.

High-Yield Primary Immunodeficiencies

Disease Defect
DiGeorge syndrome Thymic aplasia → ↓ T cells
SCID T + B/NK cell dysfunction
CVID ↓ Immunoglobulins
Selective IgA deficiency ↓ IgA

Rapid Recall

  • No thymus → DiGeorge syndrome

  • No T cells → Thymic aplasia

  • 22q11 deletion → CATCH-22

Pathology-01.question: ৪৪) Genetic derangement causing cell injury is
Pathology-01.exp:
Sickle cell anaemia is a genetic disorder caused by a mutation in the β-globin gene of haemoglobin. The abnormal haemoglobin (HbS) polymerizes under low oxygen conditions, causing red blood cell sickling and cellular injury.

It is an example of cell injury due to genetic derangement.

Option Analysis

  • ক) Anaphylactic reaction  Causes immune-mediated cell injury due to IgE-mediated hypersensitivity.

  • খ) Autoimmune disease  Causes immune-mediated injury by antibodies or T cells against self-antigens.

  • গ) Sickle cell anaemia Genetic mutation causes abnormal protein formation and cell damage.

  • ঘ) Obesity  Causes metabolic stress and inflammation, not a primary genetic cause of cell injury.

High-Yield Causes of Cell Injury

Cause Example
Genetic derangement Sickle cell anaemia
Immune reaction Autoimmune disease, anaphylaxis
Nutritional imbalance Obesity, deficiency states
Physical agents Trauma, radiation

Rapid Recall

  • Genetic cell injury → Sickle cell anaemia

  • Immune injury → Autoimmune disease/anaphylaxis

  • HbS mutation → β-globin gene

Pathology-01.question: ৪৫) Source of free radical is
Pathology-01.exp:
X-rays are a source of free radicals because ionizing radiation causes radiolysis of water, generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) such as hydroxyl radicals (•OH), which can damage DNA, proteins, and lipids.

Antioxidant Defences

  • Vitamin C (Ascorbic acid)

  • Vitamin E

  • Catalase

  • Superoxide dismutase

  • Glutathione peroxidase

Rapid Recall

  • X-ray → Free radical generation

  • Vitamin C + Catalase → Antioxidants

  • ROS → Lipid peroxidation + DNA damage

Pathology-01.question: ৪৬) Liquefactive necrosis is seen in -
Pathology-01.exp:
Liquefactive necrosis occurs when dead tissue is digested by hydrolytic enzymes, resulting in transformation into a liquid, viscous mass. It is classically seen in abscess formation due to bacterial infection.

Common sites:

  • Brain infarction (classic example)

  • Abscesses caused by bacterial infections

Rapid Recall

  • Abscess → Liquefactive necrosis

  • Heart infarct → Coagulative necrosis

  • TB granuloma → Caseous necrosis

  • Pancreatitis → Fat necrosis

Pathology-01.question: ৪৭) Enzymatic fat necrosis occurs in
Pathology-01.exp:
Enzymatic fat necrosis occurs mainly in acute pancreatitis, where pancreatic enzymes (especially lipase) leak into surrounding tissues and digest fat.

Mechanism:

  • Pancreatic lipase breaks down triglycerides → free fatty acids

  • Free fatty acids combine with calcium → fat saponification

  • Produces chalky white deposits (saponification)

Option Analysis

  • ক) Heart  Usually shows coagulative necrosis in myocardial infarction.

  • খ) Adrenal gland  Not a typical site of enzymatic fat necrosis.

  • গ) Pancreas  Classic site in acute pancreatitis.

  • ঘ) Brain  Brain infarction causes liquefactive necrosis.

Rapid Recall

  • Pancreas + lipase → Fat necrosis

  • Calcium + fatty acid → Saponification

  • Acute pancreatitis → Enzymatic fat necrosis

Pathology-01.question: ৪৮) Most characteristic feature of apoptosis is
Pathology-01.exp:
The most characteristic feature of apoptosis is the formation of apoptotic bodies. During apoptosis, the cell undergoes controlled fragmentation into membrane-bound apoptotic bodies that are rapidly removed by phagocytes without causing inflammation.

Key morphological features:

  • Cell shrinkage

  • Chromatin condensation

  • Nuclear fragmentation

  • Formation of apoptotic bodies

Option Analysis

  • ক) Chromatin condensation  A typical feature of apoptosis, but not the most characteristic final morphological feature.

  • খ) Cell shrinkage  Occurs in apoptosis but is not diagnostic.

  • গ) Formation of apoptotic bodies  Hallmark morphological feature of apoptosis.

  • ঘ) Formation of bleb  Membrane blebbing can occur, but it is not the defining feature.

High-Yield Apoptosis vs Necrosis

Feature Apoptosis Necrosis
Cell size Shrinkage Swelling
Membrane Intact Disrupted
Inflammation Absent Present
Nuclear change Chromatin condensation Karyolysis
Key feature Apoptotic bodies Cell rupture

Rapid Recall

  • Apoptosis → Apoptotic bodies

  • Necrosis → Cell swelling + inflammation

  • Apoptosis = programmed cell death

Pathology-01.question: ৪৯) Delayed type hypersensitivity excludes
Pathology-01.exp:
Reference: DavidsonDelayed-type hypersensitivity (Type IV hypersensitivity) is a T-cell mediated immune reaction. It occurs without antibodies and typically develops 24–72 hours after antigen exposure.

Examples:

  • Type 1 diabetes mellitus → T-cell mediated destruction of pancreatic β-cells

  • Acute cellular rejection → T lymphocyte-mediated graft injury

  • Hashimoto thyroiditis → T-cell mediated autoimmune thyroid destruction

Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) is an antibody-mediated (Type II hypersensitivity) disorder caused by IgG antibodies against platelet membrane glycoproteins.

Option Analysis

  • ক) Type 1 diabetes  Type IV hypersensitivity (T-cell mediated).

  • খ) Acute cellular rejection  Type IV hypersensitivity (T-cell mediated).

  • গ) Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura  Type II hypersensitivity (IgG-mediated platelet destruction).

  • ঘ) Hashimoto’s thyroiditis  Mainly T-cell mediated (Type IV).

High-Yield Hypersensitivity Types

Type Mechanism Example
Type I IgE + mast cells Anaphylaxis, asthma
Type II IgG/IgM against cells ITP, autoimmune haemolytic anaemia
Type III Immune complex SLE, serum sickness
Type IV T cells TB skin test, DM1, graft rejection

Rapid Recall

  • Delayed hypersensitivity = Type IV = T cells

  • ITP = Type II = IgG against platelets

  • Acute cellular rejection = T cells

Pathology-01.question: ৫০) Conditions where both ESR & CRP raised
Pathology-01.exp:
Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR) is a classic inflammatory condition where both ESR and CRP are markedly elevated. It is associated with systemic inflammation and usually presents with:

  • Age >50 years

  • Bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness

  • Markedly raised inflammatory markers

Option Analysis

  • ক) Sjögren’s syndrome  ESR may be elevated, but CRP is often normal because it is not a strongly acute inflammatory condition.

  • খ) Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE)  ESR is usually raised, but CRP is often normal unless there is infection or serositis.

  • গ) Multiple myeloma  ESR is typically very high due to increased immunoglobulins, but CRP is not characteristically raised.

  • ঘ) Polymyalgia rheumatica  Both ESR and CRP are elevated.

High-Yield ESR vs CRP

Condition ESR CRP
Polymyalgia rheumatica ↑↑ ↑↑
SLE flare ↑ Usually normal
Multiple myeloma ↑↑↑ Variable/normal
Infection ↑ ↑

Rapid Recall

  • PMR → High ESR + High CRP

  • SLE → High ESR, normal CRP (classically)

  • Multiple myeloma → Very high ESR
